summary: This document specifies an RTP payload format for transporting video coded with JPEG XS (ISO/IEC 21122), a low-latency, lightweight image coding system. Compared to uncompressed video it allows higher resolutions and frame rates with visually lossless quality, lower power use and very small encoding latency.

eli5.summary: This document explains how to cut up special fast-to-pack video into small network pieces for sending, so a picture arrives with almost no delay.

questions: how is jpeg xs sent over rtp
what is the video jxsv media type
what is the jpeg xs rtp payload header
subtitle: How to chop JPEG XS video frames into RTP packets so studio-grade video crosses an IP network with almost no delay.

tldr.problem: JPEG XS is a lightweight, low-latency image coding system, but its compressed frames need a standard way to be split into RTP packets, labelled, and described in session descriptions.
tldr.mechanism: Each JPEG XS stream gets its own RTP stream. A frame is split into packetization units, either one per codestream or one per slice, and every packet carries a 4-byte payload header with counters and mode bits. The video/jxsv media type and SDP parameters describe the stream.
tldr.outcome: Senders and receivers can exchange JPEG XS video over RTP in a defined way, with a 90 kHz clock and parameters for negotiating format details. Congestion and security rules come from RTP itself.

today: RFC 9134 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it is still the definition of this payload format. The IANA registration of video/jxsv is recorded in the document.

sections.title: What the Payload Format Is For
sections.content:
RFC 9134 defines how video encoded with JPEG XS (ISO/IEC 21122) is carried in the Real-time Transport Protocol, RFC 3550. JPEG XS needs very moderate computing resources and stays robust under repeated compression and decompression, and when content sources are mixed, for example when subtitles, overlays or logos are embedded.

The RFC gives typical compression ratios of 2:1 to 10:1 for visually lossless quality, depending on the source material. The delay added by encoding and decoding can be held to a fraction of a video frame, typically from a small number of lines down to below a single line.
sections.eli5: JPEG XS is a way of squeezing video that is very quick to do and undo. This document is the instruction sheet for mailing that squeezed video over a network.

sections.title: How a JPEG XS Frame Is Built
sections.content:
JPEG XS uses wavelet analysis to split each image component into bands of coefficients. Coefficients covering the same spatial region are grouped into precincts, and one or more precincts form a slice. A slice is the smallest independently decodable unit of a codestream and always spans the full width of the image, though only part of its height.

A codestream is a header starting with the SOC marker (0xff10), one or more slices, and an EOC marker (0xff11). The codestream alone gives sample values. Their meaning comes from two boxes defined in ISO/IEC 21122-3: the video support box (maximum bit rate, frame rate, interlace mode, subsampling, profile, level and sublevel) and the color specification box (color primaries, transfer characteristics, matrix coefficients, full range flag).

Boxes plus a codestream form a picture segment. A progressive frame is one picture segment. An interlaced frame is two, one per field, and both MUST carry identical boxes.
sections.eli5: A picture is cut into horizontal strips that can each be unpacked on their own. A small information card travels with the strips to say how to show them.

sections.title: Packetization Modes
sections.content:
Each JPEG XS stream travels in its own RTP stream, with its own SSRC. A frame is the unit of data handed to RTP, and it is divided into packetization units. Each packet carries part of one, and only one, unit. All packet payloads have the same size, with the possible exception of the last packet of a unit, and unit boundaries MUST coincide with payload boundaries.

Two modes exist. In codestream mode the unit is the whole picture segment, so a progressive frame has one unit and an interlaced frame has two. In slice mode the first unit is the header segment (video support box, color specification box and codestream header), followed by one unit per slice. The last slice's unit also contains the EOC marker. Slice mode is the only one that supports out-of-order transmission.

With constant bitrate and codestream mode, each frame gets a constant number of bytes and packets. Variable bitrate or slice mode needs extra measures such as slice-level rate control, padding or empty RTP packets, which the RFC leaves to the application.
sections.eli5: You can mail the whole picture as one long stack of parcels, or mail it strip by strip. Strip by strip lets the parcels arrive in any order.

sections.title: RTP Header and Payload Header
sections.content:
Most RTP header fields follow RFC 3550. The marker bit is 1 on the last packet of a frame (progressive) or field (interlaced) and 0 otherwise. The payload type is dynamically assigned. The timestamp uses a 90 kHz clock and is the sampling instant of the frame. All packets of one frame share it, and packets MUST NOT mix data from several frames.

The first four bytes of every payload form the payload header:

  • T (1 bit): 1 means packets are sent sequentially; 0 means order is not guaranteed. It is the same for the whole stream.
  • K (1 bit): 0 for codestream mode, 1 for slice mode. If T is 0, K MUST be 1.
  • L (1 bit): set on the last packet of a packetization unit. In codestream mode it equals the marker bit.
  • I (2 bits): progressive, or first or second picture segment of an interlaced frame.
  • F counter (5 bits): frame number modulo 32.
  • SEP counter (11 bits): in slice mode the slice index modulo 2047, with 2047 for the header segment. In codestream mode it extends the packet counter when that overruns.
  • P counter (11 bits): packet number within the unit, modulo 2048.
sections.eli5: Every parcel has a small label: which frame it belongs to, which strip, which parcel of that strip, and whether it is the last one.

sections.title: The video/jxsv Media Type
sections.content:
The RFC registers the media type video/jxsv. Two parameters are required: rate, which MUST be 90000, and packetmode, which MUST equal the K bit. All parameters are declarative, since the same information is also in the payload, and their values MUST be consistent with it. Receivers ignore parameters they do not recognize.

Optional parameters include transmode (default 1, sequential-only), profile, level, sublevel, depth, width and height (each from 1 to 32767), exactframerate, interlace, segmented, sampling, colorimetry, TCS and RANGE. For example, sampling takes values such as YCbCr-4:2:2, RGB or UNSPECIFIED.

Traffic shaping is RECOMMENDED to follow the Network Compatibility Model of SMPTE ST 2110-21. If it does, the session description MUST signal it with the TP parameter.
sections.eli5: The media type is a name tag for this kind of video, plus a short list of settings, like the picture size and colors, so both sides agree before starting.

sections.title: SDP Mapping and Offer/Answer
sections.content:
In the Session Description Protocol, video goes in the m= line, jxsv/90000 goes in a=rtpmap, and packetmode plus any optional parameters go in a=fmtp as a semicolon-separated list. If the SDP and the payload disagree, the payload values prevail.

In the offer/answer model (RFC 3264) for unicast, a=fmtp MUST be present and describes the sender's capabilities. An answerer that cannot support every parameter and value offered MUST reject the session. If it accepts, it replies with exactly the same values. The same payload type number SHOULD be used in the answer.
sections.eli5: Before the video starts, one side says what it will send. The other side either says yes to everything, repeating it back, or says no.

sections.title: Congestion and Security
sections.content:
Congestion control follows RFC 3550 and the RTP profile in use. JPEG XS is mainly meant for controlled networks, but may be used on best-effort ones such as the Internet. There, users MUST monitor packet loss, for example with RTCP feedback as in RFC 8888. The RFC notes that HD or UHD video can need more than 1 Gbps, enough to cause a denial of service on most Internet paths.

Security rests on RTP and its profiles, such as SRTP. Decoders and encoders must be robust against malicious or malformed payloads, because a memory overrun could lead to arbitrary code execution. The RFC finds the format unlikely to enable denial of service through pathological datagrams, and says it contains no executable code.
sections.eli5: Video this big can flood a small road. Senders must watch for lost packets, and receivers must stay safe if someone sends a broken parcel on purpose.
